title: JSON to Python Dataclass Generator Online, Free | OpenAnyDoc
description: Turn a JSON sample into Python dataclasses with type hints: int or float as seen, str | None for missing keys. Copy or download a .py file.
heading: JSON to Python Dataclasses with Type Hints
subtitle: Paste or open JSON and get Python dataclasses at once; nothing is uploaded.
intro: Give your Python code real types for the JSON it reads. Open a config file, an API response or a record from a queue, and the page writes a plain @dataclass for every object in it, in modern Python 3.10 syntax: int where the sample has whole numbers, float where it has decimals, list[str] or list[Project] for arrays, and str | None = None where a value can be missing or null. Field names are snake_case, so postalCode becomes postal_code. Copy the classes into your module or download a .py file. Everything is generated in your browser, so the data is never uploaded.

steps.title: Read the dataclasses

handlesTitle: What the JSON to Python generator handles
handles: Objects: one plain @dataclass each, with nested objects as their own classes referenced by name.
Numbers: int when every value seen is whole, float as soon as one has a decimal part.
Arrays: list[...] typed by their items, such as list[str] or list[Project]; objects in one list are merged into one dataclass.
Missing or null values: a type such as str | None with a default of None.
Names: camelCase or dashed keys become snake_case fields, such as postal_code from postalCode.
Input from a .json file, a drop, the paste box or a sample, up to 10 MB.
limits: The code needs Python 3.10 or later, because it uses list[str] and str | None.
There are no from_dict or to_dict helpers: field names are not mapped back to the JSON keys, and nested dicts are not turned into objects for you.
Types come from one sample: a field that is a whole number there but a decimal elsewhere will be typed int.
Very large documents may take a few seconds; files up to 10 MB.
faqTitle: JSON to Python dataclasses: questions and answers

faq.question: Is my file uploaded?
faq.answer: No. The JSON is read and the Python code is generated by your browser, on your device. Pasted text stays in this tab and is never sent anywhere.

faq.question: Why does a field read str | None = None?
faq.answer: Because it was null somewhere in the sample, or missing from some of the objects in an array. str | None means the field holds a string or None, and the default of None lets you leave it out.

faq.question: Can I pass my JSON straight to the dataclass?
faq.answer: Only if the keys are already snake_case. Address(**{"postalCode": "12345"}) fails because the field is postal_code. Rename the keys first, for example with a small dict comprehension, and build nested objects the same way.

faq.question: Why did a price become int instead of float?
faq.answer: Every price in your sample was a whole number, such as 10 or 25. Add one value with a decimal part, such as 10.5, and the field becomes float, or change the hint by hand.

faq.question: Which Python version do I need?
faq.answer: Python 3.10 or later. The hints use the built-in list[...] and the X | None form, which older versions do not accept at runtime.

faq.question: Why dataclasses and not Pydantic models?
faq.answer: Dataclasses are in the standard library, so the code runs with no extra package. If your project uses Pydantic, the fields carry over to a BaseModel, where an alias generator can map camelCase keys for you.

faq.question: How do I convert JSON to a Python dataclass?
faq.answer: Paste JSON into OpenAnyDoc's JSON to Python generator and the dataclasses appear at once, one per kind of object, with typed snake_case fields. Copy them or download a .py file; the JSON is turned into code in your browser without being uploaded.
